title: Surgical Pelvic Neuroanatomy, Retroperitoneal Spaces & Vascular Control

steps.say: A mastery of pelvic retroperitoneal avascular spaces is essential for safely performing radical oncologic resections without injuring pelvic vessels, ureters, or autonomic nerves. Developing the paravesical space establishes the anterior lateral surgical dissection boundary.
steps.tx: Developing the avascular **paravesical space** establishes the anterolateral pelvic dissection boundary. It is bounded laterally by the external iliac vessels and obturator internus muscle, medially by the **obliterated umbilical artery**, posteriorly by the **cardinal ligament**, and anteriorly by the pubic symphysis. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary tumor board review ensure optimal patient outcomes.

nodes.label: Incise pelvic sidewall peritoneum parallel to external iliac artery
Identify obliterated umbilical artery (medial umbilical ligament)
Bluntly develop avascular fat space down to levator ani
Expose obturator nerve and cardinal ligament anterior leaf

steps.tx: Opening the pelvic sidewall means developing spaces that contain almost no vessels when entered in the correct plane. On one side the picture shows the **paravesical space** and behind it the pararectal space, opened so the ureter, uterine artery and internal iliac branches can be identified before division. Working through these bloodless windows is what makes radical pelvic dissection controlled rather than a search through tumour distorted tissue.
steps.say: Paravesical and pararectal spaces are opened on the pelvic sidewall to expose ureter and iliac branches. Bloodless planes make radical dissection controlled.

steps.say: The avascular pararectal space provides critical access to the pelvic sidewall, hypogastric vessels, and pelvic autonomic nerve plexus. It is bounded medially by the rectum and uterosacral ligament, and laterally by the internal iliac artery.
steps.tx: The avascular **pararectal space** provides lateral pelvic sidewall exposure. It is bounded medially by the **rectum** and uterosacral ligament, laterally by the **internal iliac artery**, posteriorly by the sacrum, and anteriorly by the **cardinal ligament**; the ureter courses along its medial peritoneal leaf.  Evidence-based practice integrates cardinal ligament anterior boundary, internal iliac lateral boundary, ureter on medial leaf.

rows: Avascular cleavage plane anterior to sacrum

steps.say: The cardinal ligament represents the central fibromuscular barrier dividing the paravesical space anteriorly from the pararectal space posteriorly. It transmits the uterine artery, which crosses directly superior and anterior to the ureter roughly two centimeters lateral to the cervix.
steps.tx: The **cardinal ligament** (Mackenrodt's ligament) separates the paravesical space anteriorly from the pararectal space posteriorly. It transmits the **uterine artery**, which crosses superior and anterior to the **ureter** ('water under the bridge') approximately 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix.  Evidence-based practice integrates paravesical and pararectal boundary, uterine artery crosses ureter, 1.5-2 cm lateral to cervix.

steps.say: The presacral space lies between the parietal fascia covering the anterior sacral promontory and the visceral fascia propria of the rectum. Dissection within this retrorectal plane must avoid tearing the valveless presacral venous plexus, which causes catastrophic hemorrhage.
steps.tx: The **presacral space** (retrorectal space) lies between the anterior sacral periosteum and the visceral fascia propria of the rectum. Dissection must strictly avoid tearing the valveless **presacral venous plexus**, which retracts into sacral foramina and produces life-threatening, intractable hemorrhage. Integrated clinical protocols and evidence-based decision pathways improve overall treatment efficacy.

nodes.label: Incise posterior pelvic peritoneum over sacral promontory
Retract rectum anteriorly within intact fascia propria
Avoid blunt trauma to underlying middle sacral and presacral veins
Control unexpected bleeding with sterile titanium thumbtacks

steps.say: Bilateral ligation of the internal iliac arteries represents a lifesaving emergency surgical technique to control severe pelvic hemorrhage. Hypogastric artery ligation reduces pelvic arterial pulse pressure by eighty-five percent and total pelvic blood flow by nearly fifty percent.
steps.tx: Bilateral **internal iliac artery ligation** (hypogastric artery ligation) reduces pelvic pulse pressure by 85% and blood flow by 48%, converting a high-pressure pulsatile pelvic arterial hemorrhage into a low-pressure venous bleed controlled through extensive **collateral arterial circulation**.  Evidence-based practice integrates 85% pulse pressure reduction, 48% flow reduction, pelvic collateral circulation.

steps.say: Internal iliac artery ligation is performed three to four centimeters distal to the common iliac bifurcation. The surgeon carefully mobilizes the artery off the underlying internal iliac vein and passes a right-angle clamp from lateral to medial to avoid vessel laceration.
steps.tx: Internal iliac artery ligation is performed 3 to 4 cm distal to the common iliac bifurcation, preserving the posterior division when feasible. The surgeon passes a right-angle clamp from **lateral to medial** beneath the artery to avoid catastrophic laceration of the adherent underlying **internal iliac vein**.  Evidence-based practice integrates internal iliac ligation technique, 3-4 cm distal to bifurcation, lateral to medial clamp passage.

nodes.label: Retract ureter medially with posterior peritoneum
Identify common iliac bifurcation and external/internal branches
Pass right-angle clamp from lateral to medial beneath hypogastric artery
Place double non-absorbable ligatures without transecting vessel

steps.say: The pelvic autonomic nervous system comprises sympathetic hypogastric nerves and parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves that coalesce to form the inferior hypogastric plexus. Preserving these nerves during radical hysterectomy prevents postoperative neurogenic bladder and anorectal dysfunction.
steps.tx: The **pelvic autonomic nervous system** comprises sympathetic hypogastric nerves (from L5-S1) and parasympathetic **pelvic splanchnic nerves** (nervi erigentes, S2-S4) forming the **inferior hypogastric plexus** lateral to the rectum; nerve-sparing surgery prevents neurogenic bladder atony and severe chronic obstipation.  Evidence-based practice integrates hypogastric nerves (sympathetic), pelvic splanchnic S2-S4 (parasympathetic).

left.title: Sympathetic Hypogastric Nerves
points: Arise from superior hypogastric plexus at L5-S1
Control internal urinary sphincter and bladder filling

right.title: Parasympathetic Splanchnic Nerves
points: Emerge from anterior sacral roots S2-S4 (nervi erigentes)
Drive detrusor muscle contraction and bladder emptying

steps.say: The obturator nerve originates from the posterior divisions of the second, third, and fourth lumbar ventral rami and traverses the lateral pelvic sidewall deep to the external iliac vein. Iatrogenic transection causes loss of thigh adduction and sensory anesthesia over the medial thigh.
steps.tx: The **obturator nerve** (L2-L4 lumbar plexus) traverses the obturator fossa deep to the external iliac vein, coursing along the obturator internus muscle into the obturator canal. Iatrogenic transection results in paralysis of the **thigh adductor muscles** and sensory numbness over the medial thigh.  Evidence-based practice integrates obturator nerve L2-L4, medial thigh anesthesia.
